sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Amoghasiddhi** ​(*amoghasiddhi*) — ‌Infallible Success, ‌North · ​'Unfailing Accomplishment' ​— the ​fifth Dhyānibuddha, ​lord of ​the karma ‌family — ​belongs to ​the Buddhist ‌tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the ‌domain "Infallible ​Success, North". ​The name ​means "'Unfailing ​Accomplishment' — ​the fifth ‌Dhyānibuddha, lord ​of the ‌karma family"[^1].

​**Amoghasiddhi** — ‌'Unfailing Accomplishment' ​— is ‌the fifth ​of ‌the Five ​Meditation Buddhas ​(Dhyānibuddhas), lord ‌of the ‌karma family ‌and sovereign ​of the ​mandala's northern ‌quarter. Where ​his companions ​preside over ‌insight, anger, ​pride, and ​desire, he ‌presides ​over action ‌itself: the ​wisdom that ​completes what ​is begun. ​His raised ‌palm answers ‌fear; his ​green body, ‌the color ​of ripening, ​promises that ‌no honest ‌effort is ‌wasted.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ​the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ​**Amoghasiddhi** and ​serves its ​temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/amoghasiddhi/). ​The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *amoghasiddhi* ​contains the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics or ‌special encoding ​is claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sources.citation: Guhyasamāja Tantra, ch. III — the earliest systematic tantric mandala of the five Dhyānibuddhas, naming Amoghasiddhi in the northern seat of the karma family.

Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha (Tattvasaṃgraha Tantra) — the paradigmatic narrative of the five tathāgatas' subjugation of the unruly forces, with Amoghasiddhi presiding over the north, the wind element, and all-accomplishing wisdom.
Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti, v. 8 — the liturgical verse naming the five tathāgatas (Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi) that underlies the whole pentad system.

sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Devanagari ​as **अमोघसिद्धि**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"'Unfailing Accomplishment' ​— the ‌fifth ​Dhyānibuddha, lord ​of the ‌karma ​family"[^1].

The ‌canonical spelling ​**Amoghasiddhi** ‌matches the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. ​The plain ​ASCII form ​*amoghasiddhi* ‌contains the ​same letters, ‌so ​no lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ‌transition is ​claimed. The ‌editorial ​work is ​to fix ‌one ‌reviewed reference ‌spelling, preserve ​capitalization ​and provenance, ‌and keep ​the ​original evidence ‌visible. The ​displayed ​form is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed form ​itself.

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/amoghasiddhi/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**amoghasiddhi** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Amoghasiddhi.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Amoghasiddhi" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Amoghasiddhi" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"amoghasiddhi" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Amoghasiddhi ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Amoghasiddhi ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Amoghasiddhi ‌place infallible ​success, ​north at ​the ​center ​of a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

Amoghasiddhi ​appears ‌in buddhist ​tradition ‌as infallible ​success, ​north. The ​name's ​meaning, "'Unfailing ​Accomplishment' ‌— ​the fifth ‌Dhyānibuddha, ​lord of ‌the ​karma family", ‌shapes ​the narratives ‌told ​about this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ‌Memory ‌(Cult)

Devotees ​and ​later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ​Amoghasiddhi ​in ritual, ‌text, ​and iconography, ​ensuring ‌the name ​survived ‌into the ​modern ​scholarly record.

​The ​myths of ‌Amoghasiddhi ‌survive ​in fragments, ‌summaries, ​and later ​retellings. ‌Each version ‌reflects ‌the interests ‌of ​its tellers ‌— ​poets, priests, ​philosophers, ​and scholars. ‌The ​PuniCodex ​entry does ​not ‌privilege a ​single ​version; it ​gathers ‌the attestations ​so ‌that readers ​can ‌compare them. ​The ‌restoration Amoghasiddhi ‌gives ​the ​figure a ​stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Amoghasiddhi ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Buddhist ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming अमोघसिद्धि, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to infallible ​success ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Every ​tradition personifies ‌its favorite ‌anxiety. ​The Greeks ​made ​a goddess ​of ruin, ​the ‌Norse of ​old age; ​Buddhism ‌personified the ​fear of ‌wasted ​effort. Amoghasiddhi ‌is ​the answer ​to the ​question ​every practitioner ​asks in ‌the ​dark middle ‌of the ​work: ‌is any ​of ‌this actually ​working? His ‌name ​is the ​vow — ‌*not ‌vain, not ‌useless, infallible*.

​Look ​at what ‌his ​assigned affliction ​is: envy, ‌the ​poison of ​comparison, the ‌certainty ​that accomplishment ‌lives in ​other ​people's hands. ​His ​teaching does ‌not suppress ‌that ​energy; it ‌redirects it, ​because ​all-accomplishing wisdom ‌acts for ‌others, ‌and action ‌done ​selflessly for ‌others cannot ​fail ​— there ​is no ‌one ​left for ​it to ​fail ‌in front ​of. ​The raised ​hand is ‌not ​a trophy. ‌It is ​a ‌promise made ​to the ‌frightened, ‌by the ​one ​Buddha whose ​name is ​not ‌a description ‌but a ​guarantee.[^1]
